공감하다.nuance: 공감하다 means more than understanding the facts: it means emotionally relating to someone’s feeling, experience, or point of view. The usual target takes 에 — 그 말에 공감해요, 주인공의 마음에 공감해요 — whereas 동의하다 focuses on agreeing that an opinion or proposal is correct. You can understand someone without agreeing with them, so 이해하다, 공감하다, and 동의하다 are not interchangeable. In conversation, 공감돼요 is extremely common and presents the reaction as something that naturally ‘lands’ with you: 저도 그 부분이 공감돼요. 공감하다 is useful for films, relationships, workplace stories, and any moment when you want to say ‘I can relate.’
공감하다.explanation: 공감하다 (gonggamhada) means "to empathize with / relate to." Learn the frame N에 공감해요, not an isolated English translation. Use it when another person’s feeling or experience feels familiar to you; use 동의해요 when you are specifically agreeing with an opinion.
공감하다.shortExplanation: 공감하다 means emotionally relating to someone or something, usually in the frame N에 공감해요.
commonMistakes: Using 을/를 with the target: 그 의견을 공감해요. The standard frame is 그 의견에 공감해요.
Treating 공감하다 and 동의하다 as identical. 공감하다 is emotional identification; 동의하다 is agreement with a claim or proposal.
Using 공감해요 for simple factual comprehension. If you only mean ‘I understand the explanation,’ say 이해해요 or 알겠어요.
Saying 사람을 공감해요 as the default. More naturally, name the feeling or experience: 그 사람의 마음에 공감해요.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 → 해요
conjugationTips.body: 공감하다 is a regular 하다 verb: 공감해요, 공감했어요, 공감할 수 있어요. In casual conversation, 공감돼요 is also common when the feeling naturally resonates with you.

usagePhrases.en: I relate to what you said.
usagePhrases.note: The thing you relate to takes 에.
공감되다 is a very natural receptive form in conversation.
Focuses on the person’s emotional state.
-기 turns the verb into an activity noun before 어렵다.

examples.ko: 저도 혼자 외국에서 살아 봐서 그 마음에 공감해요.
examples.romanization: jeodo honja oegugeseo sara bwaseo geu maeume gonggamhaeyo.
examples.en: I have lived abroad alone too, so I empathize with that feeling.
examples.note: A shared experience creates the basis for empathy.

examples.ko: 그 의견에는 동의하지 않지만 왜 그렇게 느끼는지는 이해하고 그 마음에는 공감해요.
examples.romanization: geu uigyeoneneun donguihaji anchiman wae geureoke neukkineunjineun ihaehago geu maeumeneun gonggamhaeyo.
examples.en: I do not agree with that opinion, but I understand why they feel that way and empathize with them.
examples.note: Separates agreement, factual understanding, and emotional empathy in one sentence.

examples.ko: 이 드라마는 직장인의 현실을 잘 보여 줘서 공감하는 사람이 많아요.
examples.romanization: i deuramaneun jikjanginui hyeonsireul jal boyeo jwoseo gonggamhaneun sarami manayo.
examples.en: This drama shows office workers’ reality well, so many people relate to it.
examples.note: 공감하는 modifies 사람, ‘people who relate.’

실패하다.nuance: 실패하다 means that an attempt, plan, project, or goal did not achieve its intended result. The target commonly takes 에: 사업에 실패하다, 시도에 실패하다. For exams and auditions, Korean often chooses the more specific 떨어지다 or 불합격하다 instead of the heavier 시험에 실패하다. Keep 실패하다 separate from 실수하다: 실패 is an unsuccessful overall result, while 실수 is a mistake made during the process. A failed attempt can be retried; a mistake can happen even inside a successful project.
실패하다.explanation: 실패하다 (silpaehada) means "to fail." Use N에 실패하다 for the attempt or goal that did not work, and use 실패할까 봐 when fear of failure causes another action. Do not use it for every small error; that is usually 실수하다.
실패하다.shortExplanation: 실패하다 describes an unsuccessful result; 실수하다 describes a mistake during the process.
commonMistakes: Saying 시험을 실패했어요. Use 시험에 실패했어요, or more naturally for a test, 시험에 떨어졌어요.
Confusing 실패하다 with 실수하다. A typo is a 실수; an entire plan that did not work is a 실패.
Using 실패하다 whenever English says ‘fail to do.’ Often 못 + verb is more natural: 연락하지 못했어요, not 연락하는 데 실패했어요 in ordinary speech.
Writing 실패 하다 with a space. The verb is one word: 실패하다.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 실패하다 conjugates regularly: 실패해요, 실패했어요, 실패할 거예요. Before -(으)ㄹ까 봐, it becomes 실패할까 봐.

usagePhrases.note: The failed field or attempt takes 에.
A neutral way to report an unsuccessful attempt.

usagePhrases.en: I am worried that I might fail.

usagePhrases.note: Here 실패 is a noun and takes 를.

examples.ko: 첫 번째 시도는 실패했지만 두 번째에는 성공했어요.
examples.romanization: cheot beonjjae sidoneun silpaehaetjiman du beonjjaeeneun seonggonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: The first attempt failed, but the second one succeeded.
examples.note: Contrasts the result words 실패하다 and 성공하다.

examples.ko: 실패할까 봐 시작도 안 하면 아무것도 배울 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: silpaehalkka bwa sijakdo an hamyeon amugeotdo baeul su eopseoyo.
examples.en: If you do not even start because you are afraid of failing, you cannot learn anything.
examples.note: Fear of failure is the cause of not starting.

examples.ko: 발표에서 단어 하나를 잘못 말한 건 실수지만, 준비한 내용을 전혀 전달하지 못한 건 실패에 가까워요.
examples.romanization: balpyoeseo daneo hanareul jalmot malhan geon silsujiman, junbihan naeyongeul jeonhyeo jeondalhaji mothan geon silpaee gakkawoyo.
examples.en: Saying one word incorrectly in a presentation is a mistake, but failing to communicate any of the prepared content is closer to an overall failure.
examples.note: Clarifies the scale difference between one mistake and an unsuccessful overall result.

성공하다.nuance: 성공하다 means reaching a desired result in a project, career, business, experiment, or attempt. The field or task commonly takes 에: 사업에 성공하다, 다이어트에 성공하다, 예약에 성공하다. Korean often uses more specific verbs where English broadly says ‘succeed’: pass an exam is 시험에 합격하다, win a competition is 대회에서 우승하다, and a plan ‘goes well’ is 일이 잘되다. 성공하다 can sound goal-focused and substantial, while 잘되다 is the more conversational choice for something simply turning out well.
성공하다.explanation: 성공하다 (seonggonghada) means "to succeed." Use N에 성공하다 for the goal or task achieved. When the situation only ‘went well,’ 잘됐어요 may sound more natural than calling it a major success.
성공하다.shortExplanation: 성공하다 means achieving a goal, usually in the pattern N에 성공하다.
commonMistakes: Using 을/를 for the achieved task: 사업을 성공했어요. Say 사업에 성공했어요.
Saying 시험에 성공했어요 for passing an exam. The normal phrase is 시험에 합격했어요.
Confusing 성공하다 with 성공시키다. 성공하다 is intransitive; 성공시키다 means to make a project or person succeed.
Using 성공했어요 for every small thing that went smoothly. In casual speech, 잘됐어요 often fits better.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 성공하다 is regular: 성공해요, 성공했어요, 성공할 거예요. The result phrase 성공하게 되다 means circumstances led to success.

usagePhrases.note: The field of success takes 에.
A more formal collocation used in reports and news.

examples.ko: 여러 번 연습한 끝에 발표를 성공적으로 마쳤어요.
examples.romanization: yeoreo beon yeonseupan kkeute balpyoreul seonggongjeogeuro machyeosseoyo.
examples.en: After practicing many times, I finished the presentation successfully.
examples.note: 성공적으로 is the adverb ‘successfully.’

examples.ko: 예약에 성공하려면 오픈 시간에 바로 접속해야 해요.
examples.romanization: yeyage seonggongharyeomyeon opeun sigane baro jeopsokhaeya haeyo.
examples.en: To succeed in making the reservation, you need to log in right when booking opens.
examples.note: A realistic high-demand reservation context.

examples.ko: 시험에는 합격했고, 준비한 프로젝트도 잘됐어요.
examples.romanization: siheomeneun hapgyeokhaetgo, junbihan peurojekteudo jal dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: I passed the exam, and the project I prepared also went well.
examples.note: Uses more natural specific verbs instead of repeating 성공하다.

투자하다.nuance: 투자하다 is not limited to stocks or real estate. You can invest money, time, energy, or attention in a company, skill, relationship, or future goal. The resource takes 을/를 and the destination takes 에: 교육에 시간을 투자하다, 회사에 돈을 투자하다. Keep it separate from 저축하다, which means saving money for later, and 소비하다, which means spending or consuming. 투자하다 implies giving resources now because you expect future value, but the word itself does not guarantee profit or success.
투자하다.explanation: 투자하다 (tujahada) means "to invest." Build the full frame: N에 돈/시간/노력을 투자하다. The destination takes 에, and the resource being invested takes 을/를.
투자하다.shortExplanation: 투자하다 means putting money, time, or effort into something for future value.
commonMistakes: Saying 회사를 투자해요. The destination takes 에: 회사에 투자해요.
Using 투자하다 as a synonym for 저축하다. Saving cash is 저축하다; putting it into an asset or project is 투자하다.
Forgetting the invested resource: 한국어에 투자해요 can be vague. 한국어 공부에 시간을 투자해요 is clearer.
Assuming 투자 always means profit is certain. The word describes the action, not the outcome.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 투자하다 conjugates regularly: 투자해요, 투자했어요, 투자할 거예요. A decision made in advance is often 투자하기로 했어요.

examples.ko: 저는 매달 수입의 일부만 장기 투자에 사용해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun maedal suibui ilbuman janggi tujae sayonghaeyo.
examples.en: I use only part of my monthly income for long-term investing.
examples.note: A neutral example of the financial meaning, not investment advice.

examples.ko: 요즘은 운동과 수면에 더 많은 시간을 투자하고 있어요.
examples.romanization: yojeumeun undonggwa sumyeone deo maneun siganeul tujahago isseoyo.
examples.en: These days, I am investing more time in exercise and sleep.
examples.note: Shows that time and health habits can also be investment targets.

examples.ko: 그 회사에 투자하기 전에 위험과 조건을 먼저 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesae tujahagi jeone wiheomgwa jogeoneul meonjeo hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: Before investing in that company, I first checked the risks and conditions.
examples.note: A careful, non-promotional financial context.

퇴직하다.nuance: 퇴직하다 is a formal, broad verb for leaving one’s position or employment, especially in documents, company notices, benefits, and retirement contexts. 퇴사하다 specifically means leaving a company, while 은퇴하다 means retiring from an entire career or public field, and 그만두다 is the everyday ‘quit/stop.’ A person can 퇴사하다 from one company without 은퇴하다 from working life. The workplace commonly takes 에서: 회사에서 퇴직하다. 정년퇴직하다 means retiring at the official retirement age; 퇴직 후 means after leaving employment.
퇴직하다.explanation: 퇴직하다 (toejikhada) means "to retire or leave a position." It is more formal than 회사 그만두다 and broader than 퇴사하다. Choose the word by scope: one company = 퇴사하다, working career = 은퇴하다, formal employment status = 퇴직하다.
퇴직하다.shortExplanation: 퇴직하다 is a formal term for leaving employment; 퇴사하다 is leaving a company, and 은퇴하다 is retiring from a career.
commonMistakes: Using 퇴직하다 as the only translation of casual ‘I quit my job.’ In conversation, 회사 그만뒀어요 or 퇴사했어요 is often more natural.
Treating 퇴직하다 and 은퇴하다 as identical. 은퇴하다 usually ends an entire career; 퇴직하다 can mean leaving one position.
Saying 회사를 퇴직했어요 as the default. More naturally, 회사에서 퇴직했어요 or 회사를 퇴사했어요.
Confusing 퇴직금 with 월급. 퇴직금 is severance/retirement pay, not ordinary salary.

conjugationTips.title: 하다 verb
conjugationTips.body: 퇴직하다 is regular: 퇴직해요, 퇴직했어요, 퇴직할 거예요. Future circumstances are often softened as 퇴직하게 될 것 같아요.

usagePhrases.en: to retire at the mandatory retirement age
after retirement / after leaving the job
usagePhrases.note: 퇴직 functions as a noun before 후.

usagePhrases.en: to receive severance or retirement pay

examples.ko: 아버지는 올해 정년퇴직하시고 여행을 다닐 계획이에요.
examples.romanization: abeojineun olhae jeongnyeon toejikasigo yeohaengeul danil gyehoegieyo.
examples.en: My father plans to travel after retiring at the official retirement age this year.
examples.note: Honorific -시- respects the father as subject.

examples.ko: 저는 회사를 퇴사했지만 아직 은퇴한 건 아니에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hoesareul toesahaetjiman ajik euntoehan geon anieyo.
examples.en: I left the company, but I have not retired from working yet.
examples.note: Clearly separates 퇴사 from 은퇴.

examples.ko: 퇴직 후 건강보험과 연금 절차를 확인했어요.
examples.romanization: toejik hu geongangboheomgwa yeongeum jeolchareul hwaginhaesseoyo.
examples.en: After leaving my job, I checked the health-insurance and pension procedures.
examples.note: A realistic formal-administrative context without giving legal advice.

두려워하다.nuance: 두려워하다 means to fear a person, thing, change, or possible result. The feared target takes 을/를: 실패를 두려워하다, 변화를 두려워하다. Its adjective counterpart 두렵다 describes the state directly — 실패가 두려워요 — while 두려워하다 presents the person as showing or carrying that fear. 무섭다 is more common for something immediately scary, such as a horror movie, a threatening person, or a loud sound; 두렵다/두려워하다 often fits deeper or more abstract fears such as failure, change, and uncertainty.
두려워하다.explanation: 두려워하다 (duryeowohada) means "to fear / be afraid of." Use N을/를 두려워하다. For your immediate feeling, N이/가 두려워요 is also natural; for a concrete scary thing, 무서워요 may fit better.
두려워하다.shortExplanation: 두려워하다 takes the feared target with 을/를 and often describes deeper or abstract fear.
commonMistakes: Using 이/가 with the target in the verb frame: 실패가 두려워해요. Say 실패를 두려워해요, or use the adjective 실패가 두려워요.
Treating 무섭다 and 두려워하다 as exact synonyms. 무섭다 is common for immediate scariness; 두려워하다 often covers abstract fear.
Writing 두려워 하다 with a space. The lexical verb is one word: 두려워하다.
Adding -하다 to 무섭다 as 무서워하다 without noticing the subject perspective. 무서워하다 often describes someone showing fear; 무서워요 directly states the feeling.

conjugationTips.title: 두려워하다 vs 두렵다
conjugationTips.body: The verb is regular: 두려워해요, 두려워했어요. The adjective changes differently: 두렵다 → 두려워요. Match the particle: 실패를 두려워해요 / 실패가 두려워요.

usagePhrases.en: Do not be afraid of change.
usagePhrases.note: -지 마세요 forms a polite negative command.

usagePhrases.en: I am afraid of being alone.
usagePhrases.note: The adjective 두렵다 states the speaker’s feeling.

examples.ko: 저는 새로운 일을 시작할 때 실패를 너무 두려워하는 편이에요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun saeroun ireul sijakal ttae silpaereul neomu duryeowohaneun pyeonieyo.
examples.en: I tend to fear failure too much when I start something new.
examples.note: -는 편이다 describes a tendency.

examples.ko: 아이는 큰 소리를 무서워하지만 낯선 사람을 특별히 두려워하지는 않아요.
examples.romanization: aineun keun sorireul museowohajiman natseon sarameul teukbyeolhi duryeowohajineun anayo.
examples.en: The child is scared of loud noises but is not especially afraid of strangers.
examples.note: Contrasts immediate scariness and broader fear.

examples.ko: 결과가 두렵더라도 필요한 말은 해야 해요.
examples.romanization: gyeolgwaga duryeopdeorado piryohan mareun haeya haeyo.
examples.en: Even if the result is frightening, you need to say what is necessary.
examples.note: Uses the adjective 두렵다 with -더라도.

인맥.nuance: 인맥 means a network of personal connections — people you know through school, work, hobbies, or introductions who may exchange information or opportunities. It is not an internet network; that is 네트워크 or 통신망. 인맥 can be neutral or positive in 인맥이 넓다 and 인맥을 쌓다, but 인맥을 이용하다 may sound calculating if the relationship is treated only as a tool. 인연 is different: it emphasizes the meaningful connection or fate that brought people together, not the practical network itself.
인맥.explanation: 인맥 (inmaek) means "personal network / connections." Learn it with 인맥을 쌓다, 인맥이 넓다, and 인맥을 통해 알게 되다. The word describes people-links, not a technical network.
인맥.shortExplanation: 인맥 is a network of personal connections built through work, school, or social life.
commonMistakes: Using 인맥 for Wi-Fi or computer networks. Use 네트워크 or 통신망 for technical networks.
Assuming 인맥 always has a negative ‘connections and favoritism’ meaning. It can simply mean one’s professional or social network.
Saying 인맥이 많다 as the only pattern. 인맥이 넓다 is the common way to say someone is well connected.
Confusing 인맥 with 인연. 인맥 is a practical network; 인연 is a meaningful personal connection or bond.

usagePhrases.note: 쌓다 presents connections as accumulated over time.
The fixed descriptive collocation uses 넓다.

usagePhrases.en: to come to know someone through one’s network

examples.ko: 행사에 자주 참여하다 보니 자연스럽게 인맥이 넓어졌어요.
examples.romanization: haengsae jaju chamyeohada boni jayeonseureopge inmaegi neolbeojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: As I kept attending events, my network naturally grew.
examples.note: The network develops as a result, not necessarily as a calculated goal.

examples.ko: 그 회사 담당자를 친구의 인맥을 통해 소개받았어요.
examples.romanization: geu hoesa damdangjareul chinguui inmaegeul tonghae sogaebadasseoyo.
examples.en: I was introduced to the person in charge at that company through a friend’s connections.
examples.note: A neutral professional introduction through a personal network.

examples.ko: 인맥만 믿기보다 실력과 신뢰를 같이 쌓는 게 중요해요.
examples.romanization: inmaengman mitgiboda sillyeokgwa silloereul gachi ssanneun ge jungyohaeyo.
examples.en: Rather than relying only on connections, it is important to build skill and trust as well.
examples.note: Shows the potentially instrumental side without treating the word itself as negative.

눈치채다.nuance: 눈치채다 means noticing or figuring something out from indirect signs: someone’s expression, unusual behavior, a changed tone, or a small clue. It describes the moment you catch on. 눈치를 보다 is different — it is the ongoing act of watching the mood and adjusting your behavior — and 눈치가 빠르다 describes a person who catches such signals quickly. 알아차리다 is a more neutral ‘notice/realize’; 눈치채다 specifically suggests social or contextual clues. The word is commonly written as one verb, 눈치채다, although the noun phrase 눈치를 채다 is also used.
눈치채다.explanation: 눈치채다 (nunchichaeda) means "to catch on / notice from clues." Use N을/를 눈치채다 or V-는 걸 눈치채다. Do not confuse it with 눈치를 보다, which means continuously reading the room.
눈치채다.shortExplanation: 눈치채다 is the moment of realizing something from subtle clues or behavior.
commonMistakes: Confusing 눈치채다 with 눈치를 보다. 채다 is catching on; 보다 is monitoring another person’s mood.
Using 눈치채다 for a plainly visible fact with no inference. 알아차리다 or 보다 may be more neutral in that case.
Writing 눈치 체다. The verb is 채다: 눈치채다 / 눈치를 채다.
Forgetting the embedded-action pattern: 그가 거짓말했어요 눈치챘어요. Say 그가 거짓말하는 걸 눈치챘어요.

conjugationTips.title: 채다 → 채요 / 챘어요
conjugationTips.body: 눈치채다 conjugates as 눈치채요, 눈치챘어요, 눈치챌 거예요. The completed modifier is 눈치챈, as in 눈치챈 사람.

usagePhrases.en: to catch on to a secret

usagePhrases.note: A soft guess about someone’s realization.

usagePhrases.en: to notice that someone is lying
usagePhrases.note: V-는 걸 embeds the action being noticed.

examples.ko: 표정이 갑자기 바뀌어서 무슨 일이 있다는 걸 눈치챘어요.
examples.romanization: pyojeongi gapjagi bakkwieoseo museun iri itdaneun geol nunchichaesseoyo.
examples.en: Their expression suddenly changed, so I realized something was going on.
examples.note: The facial change is the indirect clue.

examples.ko: 친구가 깜짝 파티를 준비하는 걸 이미 눈치챘지만 모르는 척했어요.
examples.romanization: chinguga kkamjjak patireul junbihaneun geol imi nunchichaetjiman moreuneun cheokaesseoyo.
examples.en: I had already figured out that my friend was preparing a surprise party, but I pretended not to know.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 척하다.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 눈치가 빨라서 분위기가 어색해진 걸 바로 눈치채요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun nunchiga ppallaseo bunwigiga eosaekaejin geol baro nunchichaeyo.
examples.en: That person is socially perceptive, so they immediately notice when the mood becomes awkward.
examples.note: Connects the ability 눈치가 빠르다 with the action 눈치채다.

감추다.nuance: 감추다 is a transitive verb meaning to conceal something from sight or knowledge: 감정을 감추다, 사실을 감추다, 물건을 감추다. 숨기다 is the more frequent everyday verb and works broadly for objects, information, and feelings; 감추다 often sounds slightly more deliberate, literary, or focused on keeping something from showing. The hidden thing takes 을/를. The result can be expressed with 감춰지다 or 감추어지다, and ‘cannot hide it’ is 감출 수 없다 or 감춰지지 않다 depending on whether the focus is ability or visible result.
감추다.explanation: 감추다 (gamchuda) means "to hide / conceal." Use N을/를 감추다. It overlaps with 숨기다, but 감추다 often emphasizes deliberately keeping feelings, facts, or signs from showing.
감추다.shortExplanation: 감추다 is a transitive verb for deliberately concealing feelings, facts, or objects.
commonMistakes: Using 이/가 for the hidden thing: 감정이 감췄어요. The person hides the object, so say 감정을 감췄어요.
Treating 감추다 and 감춰지다 as the same voice. 감추다 = someone conceals it; 감춰지다 = it becomes hidden.
Writing 감추어요 as the only spoken form. It is grammatical, but the contracted 감춰요 is much more natural in conversation.
Using 감추다 for placing an item somewhere ordinary. If there is no intention to conceal it, 놓다 or 보관하다 may fit better.

conjugationTips.title: 감추다 → 감춰요
conjugationTips.body: 감추 + 어요 contracts to 감춰요. Other useful forms are 감췄어요, 감출 거예요, and 감추려고 해요.

usagePhrases.en: I tried / intended to hide it.

examples.ko: 괜찮은 척했지만 실망한 표정을 완전히 감추지는 못했어요.
examples.romanization: gwaenchaneun cheokaetjiman silmanghan pyojeongeul wanjeonhi gamchujineun mothaesseoyo.
examples.en: I pretended to be fine, but I could not completely hide my disappointed expression.
examples.note: -지는 못하다 gives a partial or qualified inability.

examples.ko: 회사는 문제를 해결하기보다 사실을 감추려고 했어요.
examples.romanization: hoesaneun munjereul haegyeolhagiboda sasireul gamchuryeogo haesseoyo.
examples.en: The company tried to conceal the facts rather than solve the problem.
examples.note: A deliberate information-concealment context.

examples.ko: 선물을 서랍 안에 감춰 뒀는데 동생이 바로 찾았어요.
examples.romanization: seonmureul seorap ane gamchwo dwonneunde dongsaengi baro chajasseoyo.
examples.en: I hid the present in a drawer, but my younger sibling found it right away.
examples.note: 감춰 두다 means hide and leave it there.

티나다.nuance: The natural expression is 티가 나다, literally ‘a sign appears’: an emotion, change, lie, effort, or imitation becomes noticeable. In casual speech the particle is often dropped — 티 나요, 너무 티 나 — and online text may join it as 티나다, but standard spacing keeps the noun and verb separate. Compare 티가 나다 with 티를 내다: 티가 나다 means it shows, often unintentionally; 티를 내다 means someone deliberately lets it show or makes a display of it. 티가 안 나다 means the difference is not noticeable and can be positive, as with natural makeup or a well-repaired item.
티나다.explanation: 티가 나다 (tiga nada) means "to show / be obvious." Learn the complete contrast: 티가 나요 (it shows), 티가 안 나요 (it is not noticeable), and 티를 내요 (someone deliberately shows it).
티나다.shortExplanation: 티가 나다 means that a feeling, change, or lie becomes visibly noticeable.
commonMistakes: Writing the standard phrase only as 티나다. In careful writing, use 티가 나다 or the particle-dropped 티 나다.
Confusing 티가 나다 with 티를 내다. 가 나다 is an appearing sign; 를 내다 is deliberately showing it.
Using 티가 보이다 as the default. It is understandable, but the fixed everyday expression is 티가 나다.
Assuming 티가 나다 is always negative. ‘수선한 티가 안 나요’ and ‘노력한 티가 나요’ can be compliments.

usagePhrases.note: The particle 가 is commonly dropped in speech.

usagePhrases.en: to show signs of having lied
usagePhrases.note: The modifier names what kind of sign shows.
티를 내다 is deliberate, unlike 티가 나다.

examples.ko: 괜찮다고 했지만 목소리에서 속상한 티가 났어요.
examples.romanization: gwaenchantago haetjiman moksorieseo soksanghan tiga nasseoyo.
examples.en: They said they were fine, but their voice showed that they were upset.
examples.note: The voice gives away the hidden feeling.

examples.ko: 화장을 아주 자연스럽게 해서 거의 티가 안 나요.
examples.romanization: hwajangeul aju jayeonseureopge haeseo geoui tiga an nayo.
examples.en: The makeup is very natural, so it is hardly noticeable.
examples.note: A positive use of 티가 안 나다.

examples.ko: 모르는 척했는데 이미 다 아는 티가 났나 봐요.
examples.romanization: moreuneun cheokaenneunde imi da aneun tiga nanna bwayo.
examples.en: I pretended not to know, but I guess it was obvious that I already knew everything.
examples.note: Pairs naturally with 척하다 and -나 봐요.

취소되다.nuance: 취소되다 is the passive/intransitive side of 취소하다. The event, appointment, order, or reservation that no longer happens becomes the subject with 이/가: 행사가 취소됐어요, 예약이 취소됐어요. If a person actively cancels something, use 을/를 + 취소하다: 제가 예약을 취소했어요. Do not confuse cancellation with postponement: 연기되다 means it will happen later, while 취소되다 means the plan is no longer going ahead. 변경되다 means details changed but the event may still happen.
취소되다.explanation: 취소되다 (chwisodoeda) means "to be canceled." Use N이/가 취소되다 for the canceled event, and N을/를 취소하다 when someone actively cancels it.
취소되다.shortExplanation: 취소되다 is passive: the canceled plan takes 이/가; the person who cancels uses 취소하다 with 을/를.
commonMistakes: Saying 행사를 취소됐어요. Passive 취소되다 needs a subject: 행사가 취소됐어요.
Using 취소되다 when the event is merely moved to a later date. That is 연기되다.
Writing 취소됬어요. The correct spelling is 취소됐어요, from 되어 → 돼.
Mixing active and passive roles: 제가 취소됐어요 normally means ‘I was canceled,’ not ‘I canceled it.’ Say 제가 예약을 취소했어요.

conjugationTips.title: 되다 → 돼요
conjugationTips.body: 취소되다 contracts in speech and writing: 취소돼요, 취소됐어요, 취소될 거예요. Keep 되어/돼 straight: 취소되어요 contracts to 취소돼요.

usagePhrases.note: The canceled plan is the subject.
Active 취소하다 takes the object 를.
취소된 is the completed modifier form.

examples.ko: 비 때문에 야외 공연이 갑자기 취소됐어요.
examples.romanization: bi ttaemune yaoe gongyeoni gapjagi chwisodwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The outdoor performance was suddenly canceled because of the rain.
examples.note: The performance is the subject of the passive verb.

examples.ko: 수업은 취소된 게 아니라 다음 주로 연기됐어요.
examples.romanization: sueobeun chwisodoen ge anira daeum juro yeongidwaesseoyo.
examples.en: The class was not canceled; it was postponed until next week.
examples.note: Directly contrasts cancellation and postponement.

examples.ko: 제가 예약을 취소했는데 환불은 아직 처리되지 않았어요.
examples.romanization: jega yeyageul chwisohanneunde hwanbureun ajik cheoridoeji anasseoyo.
examples.en: I canceled the reservation, but the refund has not been processed yet.
examples.note: Active cancellation by the speaker, followed by another passive process.

야식.nuance: 야식 is food eaten late at night, usually after the normal evening meal. It can be a small snack, but in Korean life it is often a full delivery meal such as chicken, tteokbokki, ramen, or jokbal, so ‘midnight snack’ can understate it. 간식 is any snack between meals at any time; 야식 is defined by the late-night timing. Natural verbs are 야식을 먹다 and 야식을 시키다, and people commonly ask 오늘 야식 뭐 먹지? when choosing delivery food at night.
야식.explanation: 야식 (yasik) means "late-night food / a late-night meal." Use 야식을 먹다 for eating it and 야식을 시키다 for ordering delivery. It does not have to be exactly at midnight.
야식.shortExplanation: 야식 is food eaten late at night after dinner, often a full delivery meal rather than a tiny snack.
commonMistakes: Assuming 야식 must be eaten exactly at midnight. Any noticeably late meal after dinner can be 야식.
Treating 야식 and 간식 as identical. 간식 can be an afternoon snack; 야식 is specifically late at night.
Saying 야식을 주문해요 is fine, but for casual delivery conversation 야식 시켜요 is often more natural.
Using 아침/점심/저녁-style time particles with 야식 as if it were only a time. 야식 usually names the food/meal and takes 을/를.

usagePhrases.note: 시키다 is common for ordering food delivery.
Used when choosing what to order.

usagePhrases.en: What should we eat for a late-night meal tonight?

examples.ko: 밤 열한 시에 치킨을 시켜서 야식으로 먹었어요.
examples.romanization: bam yeolhan sie chikineul sikyeoseo yasigeuro meogeosseoyo.
examples.en: We ordered chicken at eleven at night and ate it as a late-night meal.
examples.note: 야식으로 marks the role of the food.

examples.ko: 저는 오후에 먹는 간식은 괜찮지만 야식을 먹으면 잠이 잘 안 와요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun ohue meongneun gansigeun gwaenchanjiman yasigeul meogeumyeon jami jal an wayo.
examples.en: Afternoon snacks are fine for me, but if I eat late at night, I have trouble sleeping.
examples.note: Contrasts 간식 and 야식 by time.

examples.ko: 야식을 끊으려고 했는데 친구가 떡볶이 사진을 보내서 실패했어요.
examples.romanization: yasigeul kkeuneuryeogo haenneunde chinguga tteokbokki sajineul bonaeseo silpaehaesseoyo.
examples.en: I tried to stop eating late-night food, but my friend sent a photo of tteokbokki, so I failed.
examples.note: A light, realistic chat scenario.

쌓이다.nuance: 쌓이다 is the intransitive/passive counterpart of 쌓다. Things pile up or accumulate by themselves: 일이 쌓이다, 스트레스가 쌓이다, 경험이 쌓이다. If a person actively builds or stacks something, use 쌓다 with 을/를: 경험을 쌓다, 상자를 쌓다. The word works for physical piles and abstract accumulation, including dust, messages, work, fatigue, trust, and experience. Because the process is gradual, it pairs naturally with 점점, 계속, and -(으)ㄹ수록.
쌓이다.explanation: 쌓이다 (ssahida) means "to pile up / accumulate." The accumulated thing takes 이/가. Use 쌓다 with 을/를 when someone actively builds the pile or experience.
쌓이다.shortExplanation: 쌓이다 is intransitive accumulation (N이 쌓이다); 쌓다 is active building (N을 쌓다).
commonMistakes: Saying 경험을 쌓여요. Accumulation uses 경험이 쌓여요; active building uses 경험을 쌓아요.
Confusing 쌓이다 with 쌓다. The -이- form focuses on the thing accumulating, not the person doing it.
Writing 싸이다 because that matches the pronunciation. The spelling remains 쌓이다.
Using 쌓이다 only for physical objects. It is extremely common with stress, work, messages, trust, and experience.

conjugationTips.title: 쌓이다 → 쌓여요
conjugationTips.body: 쌓이 + 어요 contracts to 쌓여요. Other useful forms are 쌓였어요, 쌓일 거예요, and 쌓일수록.

usagePhrases.note: The accumulated thing is the subject.

usagePhrases.en: A lot of work has piled up.
usagePhrases.note: Common after an absence or busy period.
Pairs with gradual change in the second clause.

examples.ko: 휴가를 다녀왔더니 읽지 않은 메일이 잔뜩 쌓여 있었어요.
examples.romanization: hyugareul danyeowatdeoni ikji aneun meiri jantteuk ssayeo isseosseoyo.
examples.en: When I came back from vacation, a lot of unread emails had piled up.
examples.note: Physical/digital accumulation after time away.

examples.ko: 스트레스가 쌓이기 전에 잠깐 쉬는 게 좋아요.
examples.romanization: seuteureseuga ssahigi jeone jamkkan swineun ge joayo.
examples.en: It is good to take a short break before stress builds up.
examples.note: -기 전에 marks ‘before accumulation.’

examples.ko: 경험이 쌓일수록 어떤 문제부터 해결해야 하는지 보여요.
examples.romanization: gyeongheomi ssailssurok eotteon munjebuteo haegyeolhaeya haneunji boyeoyo.
examples.en: The more experience you gain, the more clearly you can see which problem to solve first.
examples.note: A natural proportional-development sentence.

매력.nuance: 매력 is the quality that draws people in: charm, appeal, or attractiveness. It can describe appearance, personality, a neighborhood, a language, a product, or even a difficult hobby. It is broader than 외모 or 예쁨 because something can be imperfect but still have 매력. 장점 means an objective advantage or strength; 매력 is the subjective appeal that makes you like or want to know something more. Core patterns are 매력이 있다, 매력을 느끼다, and 매력적이다.
매력.explanation: 매력 (maengnyeok) means "charm / appeal." Say 매력이 있어요 for having appeal and N의 매력을 느껴요 for feeling attracted to a quality. Do not turn it directly into a 하다 verb.
매력.shortExplanation: 매력 is the appealing quality that draws someone in, not only physical beauty.
commonMistakes: Saying 매력을 있어요. With 있다, the quality is the subject: 매력이 있어요.
Inventing 매력하다. Use 매력이 있다, 매력을 느끼다, or 매력적이다.
Treating 매력 as only physical attractiveness. A place, voice, idea, or personality can also have 매력.
Confusing 매력 with 장점. 장점 is a practical strength; 매력 is the subjective pull or charm.

usagePhrases.note: The quality takes 이 as subject.
The appeal is experienced as an object.
매력적이다 becomes 매력적인 before a noun.
Often used for something not conventionally perfect.

examples.ko: 그 카페는 화려하지 않지만 오래된 분위기 특유의 매력이 있어요.
examples.romanization: geu kapeneun hwaryeohaji anchiman oraedoen bunwigi teugyui maengnyeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: That café is not flashy, but its old-fashioned atmosphere has a distinctive charm.
examples.note: Appeal can come from a place’s distinctive atmosphere rather than conventional beauty.

examples.ko: 처음에는 어려웠지만 배우면 배울수록 한국어의 매력을 느껴요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumeneun eoryeowotjiman baeumyeon baeulsurok hangugeoui maengnyeogeul neukkyeoyo.
examples.en: It was difficult at first, but the more I learn, the more I appreciate the appeal of Korean.
examples.note: Pairs 매력 with proportional discovery.

examples.ko: 그 사람의 가장 큰 매력은 솔직하면서도 따뜻한 말투예요.
examples.romanization: geu saramui gajang keun maengnyeogeun soljikhamyeonseodo ttatteuthan maltuyeyo.
examples.en: That person’s greatest charm is a way of speaking that is honest yet warm.
examples.note: A personality-based use rather than appearance.

폐지되다.nuance: 폐지되다 means that an official system, rule, service, institution, or regularly produced program is abolished or discontinued. It is stronger and more institutional than 취소되다. A one-time appointment or event is 취소되다; a policy or recurring program that is ended is 폐지되다. 중단되다 means operation stopped, possibly temporarily, and 종영하다 means a broadcast series reached its end. The abolished item takes 이/가, while the authority actively abolishes it with 을/를 + 폐지하다.
폐지되다.explanation: 폐지되다 (pyejidoeda) means "to be abolished / discontinued." Use it for systems, rules, services, and recurring programs, not for an ordinary canceled appointment.
폐지되다.shortExplanation: 폐지되다 is an official or lasting discontinuation of a system, rule, service, or program.
commonMistakes: Using 폐지되다 for a single canceled reservation or meeting. Use 취소되다 for one-time plans.
Saying 제도를 폐지됐어요. Passive voice requires 제도가 폐지됐어요.
Treating 폐지되다 and 중단되다 as identical. 중단 may be temporary; 폐지 means the system itself is ended.
Writing 폐지됬어요. The correct form is 폐지됐어요.

conjugationTips.title: 되다 → 돼요
conjugationTips.body: 폐지되다 becomes 폐지돼요, 폐지됐어요, 폐지될 예정이에요. The active counterpart is 폐지하다.

usagePhrases.note: Used for a bus/train route permanently removed.

usagePhrases.en: It is scheduled to be discontinued starting next month.

examples.ko: 이 할인 제도는 이용자가 적어서 다음 달에 폐지될 예정이에요.
examples.romanization: i harin jedoneun iyongjaga jeogeoseo daeum dare pyejidoel yejeongieyo.
examples.en: This discount program is scheduled to be abolished next month because few people use it.
examples.note: A continuing system, so 폐지되다 fits.

examples.ko: 오늘 행사는 취소됐지만 행사 자체가 폐지된 건 아니에요.
examples.romanization: oneul haengsaneun chwisodwaetjiman haengsa jachega pyejidoen geon anieyo.
examples.en: Today’s event was canceled, but the event series itself has not been discontinued.
examples.note: Directly contrasts a one-time cancellation with abolition.

examples.ko: 버스 노선이 갑자기 폐지돼서 다른 교통편을 찾아야 했어요.
examples.romanization: beoseu noseoni gapjagi pyejidwaseo dareun gyotongpyeoneul chajaya haesseoyo.
examples.en: The bus route was suddenly discontinued, so I had to find another way to travel.
examples.note: A practical daily-life consequence of a discontinued service.

익숙해지다.nuance: 익숙해지다 describes the change from unfamiliar to familiar: you gradually get used to a place, routine, language, person’s style, or way of doing something. 익숙하다 is the resulting state (‘be familiar/accustomed’), while 익숙해지다 includes the process of becoming that way. The target normally takes 에: 한국 생활에 익숙해지다, 새 시스템에 익숙해지다. For an activity, use V-는 데 익숙해지다: 혼자 운전하는 데 익숙해졌어요. 친숙해지다 is closer to becoming familiar or friendly with something/someone, while 익숙해지다 emphasizes practical adaptation through repetition.
익숙해지다.explanation: 익숙해지다 (iksukhaejida) means "to get used to / become familiar with." Use N에 익숙해지다 or V-는 데 익숙해지다. The state after the change is 익숙하다.
익숙해지다.shortExplanation: 익숙해지다 is the process of getting used to something; 익숙하다 is the resulting state.
commonMistakes: Using 을/를 for the target: 한국 생활을 익숙해졌어요. Say 한국 생활에 익숙해졌어요.
Confusing 익숙하다 and 익숙해지다. 지금 익숙해요 is a state; 점점 익숙해지고 있어요 is a change in progress.
Saying 하는 것을 익숙해졌어요. The natural activity frame is 하는 데 익숙해졌어요.
Writing 익숙해 지다 with a space. The compound verb is written 익숙해지다.

conjugationTips.title: 해지다 → 해져요
conjugationTips.body: 익숙해지다 contracts to 익숙해져요, 익숙해졌어요, 익숙해질 거예요. The stem preserves 해지- before consonant endings: 익숙해지고 있어요.

usagePhrases.en: to get used to life in Korea
I am gradually getting used to it.
It takes time to get used to it.
usagePhrases.note: -는 데 turns the process into a time-taking activity.

usagePhrases.en: I got used to doing it alone.
usagePhrases.note: V-는 데 marks the activity adapted to.

examples.ko: 처음에는 지하철 환승이 복잡했지만 이제 많이 익숙해졌어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeumeneun jihacheol hwanseungi bokjaphaetjiman ije mani iksukhaejyeosseoyo.
examples.en: Subway transfers were confusing at first, but now I have gotten quite used to them.
examples.note: A common adaptation experience in Korea.

examples.ko: 새 프로그램에 익숙해지는 데 일주일 정도 걸렸어요.
examples.romanization: sae peurogeuraeme iksukhaejineun de iljuil jeongdo geollyeosseoyo.
examples.en: It took about a week to get used to the new program.
examples.note: Combines target 에 with the process phrase -는 데.

examples.ko: 매일 조금씩 말하다 보면 존댓말에도 자연스럽게 익숙해질 거예요.
examples.romanization: maeil jogeumssik malhada bomyeon jondaetmaredo jayeonseureopge iksukhaejil geoyeyo.
examples.en: If you keep speaking a little every day, you will naturally get used to polite Korean too.
examples.note: -다 보면 expresses adaptation through repeated experience.

예쁜.nuance: 예쁜 is the noun-modifying form of 예쁘다, so it must be followed by a noun: 예쁜 가방, 예쁜 색, 예쁜 사람. Korean descriptive verbs use -(으)ㄴ before a noun in the present state; 예쁘다 loses ㅡ and becomes 예쁜, never 예쁘는. 예쁘다 is the everyday word for something visually pretty, cute, or pleasing. 아름다운 can sound broader, more elevated, or emotionally beautiful, while 귀여운 specifically means cute. Because 예쁜 directly evaluates appearance, using it about a person is friendly but can feel personal depending on the relationship.
예쁜.explanation: 예쁜 (yeppeun) means "pretty" before a noun. It comes from 예쁘다 + -(으)ㄴ: 예쁜 가방. Use 예뻐요 when the description finishes the sentence, and 예쁜 when a noun follows.
예쁜.shortExplanation: 예쁜 is the present adjective modifier of 예쁘다: 예쁜 + noun.
commonMistakes: Saying 예쁘는 가방. Descriptive verbs use -(으)ㄴ, so the correct form is 예쁜 가방.
Using 예쁜 as a complete sentence: 이 가방 예쁜. Say 이 가방 예뻐요 or 이건 예쁜 가방이에요.
Writing 예쁘은. The ㅡ drops before ㄴ, producing 예쁜.
Treating 예쁜 and 귀여운 as identical. 예쁜 is pretty; 귀여운 is cute.

conjugationTips.title: 예쁘다 → 예쁜
conjugationTips.body: For a present descriptive modifier, add -(으)ㄴ. 예쁘다 ends in ㅡ, so ㅡ drops: 예쁘 + ㄴ → 예쁜. Predicate form: 예뻐요.

usagePhrases.note: The modifier comes directly before the noun.
Common in shopping and design talk.
예쁘게 is the adverb form, not the noun modifier.
Use the predicate form when no noun follows.

examples.ko: 친구 생일 선물로 예쁜 머그컵을 샀어요.
examples.romanization: chingu saengil seonmullo yeppeun meogeukeobeul sasseoyo.
examples.en: I bought a pretty mug as a birthday present for my friend.
examples.note: 예쁜 modifies the object 머그컵.

examples.ko: 이 색도 예쁘지만 저는 조금 더 어두운 색을 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: i saekdo yeppeujiman jeoneun jogeum deo eoduun saegeul chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: This color is pretty too, but I am looking for a slightly darker one.
examples.note: Predicate 예쁘지만 contrasts with another preference.

examples.ko: 사진에서는 예쁜데 실제로 보면 생각보다 커요.
examples.romanization: sajineseoneun yeppeunde siljero bomyeon saenggakboda keoyo.
examples.en: It looks pretty in the photo, but in person it is bigger than expected.
examples.note: A realistic online-shopping comparison.

큰.nuance: 큰 is the noun-modifying form of 크다. It can describe physical size (큰 가방), seriousness (큰 문제), importance or impact (큰 변화), and a broad amount or degree (큰 도움). Because 크다 is a descriptive verb, the present modifier is 큰, not 크는. The sentence-ending form is 커요. Do not assume every English ‘big’ maps mechanically to 큰: a large number is 큰 수, but a loud sound is 큰 소리 and a high price is 비싼 가격, not 큰 가격 in ordinary speech.
큰.explanation: 큰 (keun) means "big / large" before a noun. It comes from 크다 + ㄴ. Use 큰 가방 when a noun follows and 가방이 커요 when the description ends the sentence.
큰.shortExplanation: 큰 is the present adjective modifier of 크다 and can describe size, seriousness, or impact.
commonMistakes: Saying 크는 가방 for a bag that is currently large. 크는 means ‘growing’; the size adjective is 큰 가방.
Writing 크은. A vowel-final stem takes ㄴ: 크다 → 큰.
Using 큰 as a complete polite sentence. Say 커요 when no noun follows.
Translating every English ‘big’ with 큰. ‘Expensive price’ is 비싼 가격, not usually 큰 가격.

conjugationTips.title: 크다 → 큰 / 커요
conjugationTips.body: Before a noun, 크다 takes ㄴ and becomes 큰. Before -어요, ㅡ drops and the predicate becomes 커요.

usagePhrases.note: 큰 can mark seriousness, not only dimensions.
Predicate form without a following noun.

examples.ko: 노트북이 들어가는 큰 가방을 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: noteubugi deureoganeun keun gabangeul chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I am looking for a large bag that fits a laptop.
examples.note: Size is tied to a practical requirement.

examples.ko: 시간을 잘못 확인한 게 가장 큰 문제였어요.
examples.romanization: siganeul jalmot hwaginhan ge gajang keun munjeyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The biggest problem was that I checked the time incorrectly.
examples.note: 큰 marks seriousness/importance.

examples.ko: 처음 한국에 왔을 때 친구의 도움이 정말 컸어요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum hanguge wasseul ttae chinguui doumi jeongmal keosseoyo.
examples.en: When I first came to Korea, my friend’s help made a huge difference.
examples.note: Predicate 컸어요 expresses a large impact.

작은.nuance: 작은 is the noun-modifying form of 작다. It describes physical size (작은 방), limited amount or scale (작은 회사, 작은 실수), or a low/soft degree (작은 목소리). Since 작다 ends in a consonant, the present descriptive modifier uses -은: 작은. It is different from 적은, which means ‘few/little in quantity’: 작은 가방 is a physically small bag, while 적은 돈 is a small amount of money.
작은.explanation: 작은 (jageun) means "small" before a noun. It comes from 작다 + 은. Use 작은 방 for size, but use 적은 사람/돈 when the point is a small quantity.
작은.shortExplanation: 작은 is the modifier of 작다 for small size or scale; 적은 describes a small quantity.
commonMistakes: Saying 작는 가방. A consonant-final descriptive stem takes -은: 작은 가방.
Confusing 작은 and 적은. 작은 사람 is a small person; 적은 사람 means few people.
Using 작은 as a full sentence. Say 방이 작아요 when no noun follows.
Writing 작안 or 자근 by sound. The correct spelling is 작은.

conjugationTips.title: 작다 → 작은
conjugationTips.body: 작다 has a consonant-final stem, so add -은 before a noun: 작 + 은 → 작은. Predicate form: 작아요.

examples.ko: 주머니에 들어가는 작은 지갑이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: jumeonie deureoganeun jageun jigabi piryohaeyo.
examples.en: I need a small wallet that fits in my pocket.
examples.note: A practical shopping requirement.

examples.ko: 작은 실수였지만 고객에게 바로 설명했어요.
examples.romanization: jageun silsuyeotjiman gogaege baro seolmyeonghaesseoyo.
examples.en: It was a small mistake, but I explained it to the customer right away.
examples.note: 작은 marks the limited scale of the error.

examples.ko: 회의실이 생각보다 작아서 열 명이 앉기 어려워요.
examples.romanization: hoeuisiri saenggakboda jagaseo yeol myeongi anjgi eoryeowoyo.
examples.en: The meeting room is smaller than expected, so it is hard for ten people to sit there.
examples.note: Predicate 작아서 gives the reason.

새로운.nuance: 새로운 is the noun-modifying form of 새롭다, a ㅂ-irregular descriptive verb: 새롭다 → 새로운. It often means new in the sense of different, unfamiliar, newly introduced, or novel — 새로운 방법, 새로운 환경. The shorter 새 also comes directly before nouns and often means a newly acquired or brand-new item: 새 가방, 새 휴대폰. The two overlap, but 새로운 tends to highlight newness as a quality or change, while 새 often simply identifies the new item.
새로운.explanation: 새로운 (saeroun) means "new / novel" before a noun. It comes from the ㅂ-irregular 새롭다. Compare 새로운 방법 (a new/different method) with 새 가방 (a newly bought or brand-new bag).
새로운.shortExplanation: 새로운 is the ㅂ-irregular modifier of 새롭다 and often emphasizes a new or different quality.
commonMistakes: Writing 새롭은. Because 새롭다 is ㅂ-irregular, the correct modifier is 새로운.
Saying 새로운다 before a noun. The modifier already ends in -운: 새로운 방법.
Assuming 새 and 새로운 are always perfectly interchangeable. 새 often labels a new item; 새로운 often stresses novelty or change.
Using 새로운 as a complete sentence. Say 새로워요 when the description ends the sentence.

conjugationTips.title: 새롭다 → 새로운
conjugationTips.body: The final ㅂ changes to 우 before -(으)ㄴ: 새롭 + 은 → 새로운. Predicate form: 새로워요.

usagePhrases.note: Highlights a different or novel approach.
새 is a shorter noun modifier for a newly acquired item.

examples.ko: 기존 방식이 불편해서 새로운 예약 방법을 도입했어요.
examples.romanization: gijon bangsigi bulpyeonhaeseo saeroun yeyak bangbeobeul doiphaesseoyo.
examples.en: The old method was inconvenient, so we introduced a new booking method.
examples.note: 새로운 stresses a different system.

examples.ko: 새 휴대폰을 샀는데 기능은 생각보다 새롭지 않아요.
examples.romanization: sae hyudaeponeul sanneunde gineungeun saenggakboda saeropji anayo.
examples.en: I bought a new phone, but its features are not as innovative as I expected.
examples.note: Contrasts newly acquired 새 with novel-quality 새롭다.

examples.ko: 새로운 사람들과 일하다 보니 다른 관점을 배우게 됐어요.
examples.romanization: saeroun saramdeulgwa ilhada boni dareun gwanjeomeul baeuge dwaesseoyo.
examples.en: Working with new people led me to learn different perspectives.
examples.note: A new social environment creates a result.

좋은.nuance: 좋은 is the noun-modifying form of 좋다: 좋은 사람, 좋은 방법, 좋은 날씨. It means the noun itself is good, suitable, favorable, or high quality. Do not confuse it with 좋아하는, which means ‘that someone likes’: 좋은 영화 is a good movie, while 제가 좋아하는 영화 is a movie I like. A very useful extension is V-기 좋은 N, meaning a noun that is good/suitable for doing something: 들기 좋은 가방, 걷기 좋은 날씨. The sentence-ending form is 좋아요.
좋은.explanation: 좋은 (joeun) means "good" before a noun. Use 좋은 + noun for quality and 좋아하는 + noun for personal preference. The pattern V-기 좋은 N means "a noun suitable for doing V."
좋은.shortExplanation: 좋은 describes a good noun; 좋아하는 describes something someone likes.
commonMistakes: Saying 좋는 사람. The descriptive modifier is 좋은 사람.
Confusing 좋은 영화 with 좋아하는 영화. The first is objectively/qualitatively good; the second is one you like.
Using 좋은 as a complete sentence. Say 좋아요 when no noun follows.
Misreading 들기 좋은 가방 as ‘a bag that likes carrying.’ V-기 좋은 means suitable/easy for doing the action.

conjugationTips.title: 좋다 → 좋은
conjugationTips.body: 좋다 takes -은 before a noun: 좋은. The polite predicate is 좋아요. For preference, use 좋아하다 → 좋아하는.

usagePhrases.en: weather that is good for walking

examples.ko: 이 가방은 가볍고 튼튼해서 출근할 때 들기 좋아요.
examples.romanization: i gabangeun gabyeopgo teunteunhaeseo chulgeunhal ttae deulgi joayo.
examples.en: This bag is light and sturdy, so it is good for carrying to work.
examples.note: The V-기 좋다 suitability pattern.

examples.ko: 좋은 식당과 제가 좋아하는 식당이 항상 같은 건 아니에요.
examples.romanization: joeun sikdanggwa jega joahaneun sikdangi hangsang gateun geon anieyo.
examples.en: A good restaurant and a restaurant I personally like are not always the same.
examples.note: Directly separates quality from preference.

examples.ko: 오늘은 날씨가 좋아서 밖에서 이야기하기 좋은 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: oneureun nalssiga joaseo bakkeseo iyagihagi joeun geot gatayo.
examples.en: The weather is nice today, so it seems like a good day to talk outside.
examples.note: Combines predicate 좋다 with the suitability construction.

나쁜.nuance: 나쁜 is the noun-modifying form of 나쁘다: 나쁜 습관, 나쁜 날씨, 나쁜 선택. It can describe poor quality, harmful effects, an unfavorable situation, or moral wrongdoing. Calling a person 나쁜 사람 is a strong judgment of character, so Korean often softens criticism with 안 좋은 사람/인상/상황 when the meaning is merely unfavorable rather than morally bad. The predicate form is 나빠요, and the comparative result ‘got worse’ is 나빠졌어요.
나쁜.explanation: 나쁜 (nappeun) means "bad" before a noun. It comes from 나쁘다. Use 안 좋은 when you want a softer ‘not good’ rather than a strong moral or absolute judgment.
나쁜.shortExplanation: 나쁜 is the modifier of 나쁘다; 안 좋은 is often a softer alternative.
commonMistakes: Saying 나쁘는 습관. The correct descriptive modifier is 나쁜 습관.
Writing 나쁘은. The ㅡ drops before ㄴ, producing 나쁜.
Calling someone 나쁜 사람 when you only mean they made one poor choice. It judges the whole person strongly.
Using 나쁜 as a complete sentence. Say 상태가 나빠요 or 상황이 안 좋아요.

conjugationTips.title: 나쁘다 → 나쁜 / 나빠요
conjugationTips.body: Before ㄴ, ㅡ drops: 나쁘 + ㄴ → 나쁜. Before -아요, it becomes 나빠요. Change of state: 나빠지다.

usagePhrases.note: Softer than an absolute 나쁜 인상 in many contexts.

examples.ko: 늦게 자는 나쁜 습관을 조금씩 고치고 있어요.
examples.romanization: neutge janeun nappeun seupgwaneul jogeumssik gochigo isseoyo.
examples.en: I am gradually fixing my bad habit of going to bed late.
examples.note: A habit is modified by both a clause and 나쁜.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 나쁜 사람이라기보다 그날 기분이 안 좋았던 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: geu sarami nappeun saramiragiboda geunal gibuni an joatdeon geot gatayo.
examples.en: Rather than being a bad person, I think they were just in a bad mood that day.
examples.note: Avoids an overly broad character judgment.

examples.ko: 날씨가 나빠져서 배가 출발하지 못했어요.
examples.romanization: nalssiga nappajyeoseo baega chulbalhaji mothaesseoyo.
examples.en: The weather got worse, so the boat could not depart.
examples.note: 나빠지다 describes a worsening condition.

찾는.nuance: 찾는 is the present/habitual noun-modifying form of 찾다. It can describe something someone is currently looking for (제가 찾는 가방), a person someone asks for (사장님을 찾는 손님), or an item people frequently choose and request (손님이 많이 찾는 모델). The subject of 찾다 comes before the modifier clause, and the noun being modified comes after it. Compare 찾는 with 찾은: 찾는 물건 is the thing you are looking for; 찾은 물건 is the thing you found.
찾는.explanation: 찾는 (channeun) means "that someone is looking for / frequently asks for." It comes from 찾다 + 는. Use 찾은 for a completed result: 찾은 열쇠, ‘the key that was found.’
찾는.shortExplanation: 찾는 is the present/habitual modifier of 찾다; 찾은 marks a completed finding.
commonMistakes: Using 찾은 for something you are still looking for. 찾는 물건 = sought item; 찾은 물건 = found item.
Saying 찾다 가방. A verb must take a modifier ending before a noun: 찾는 가방.
Putting the subject after the noun: 모델 손님이 찾는. The natural order is 손님이 찾는 모델.
Assuming 찾는 always means physically searching. In 손님이 많이 찾는 메뉴, it means frequently choosing/requesting.

conjugationTips.title: 찾다 → 찾는 / 찾은
conjugationTips.body: Present or habitual action takes -는: 찾는. Completed action takes -(으)ㄴ: 찾은. Pronunciation assimilates to [찬는], but spelling stays 찾는.

usagePhrases.en: the bag I am looking for
usagePhrases.note: The subject 제가 sits inside the modifier clause.

usagePhrases.en: a menu item customers often order
a person looking for the owner
usagePhrases.note: The sought person takes 을/를 inside the clause.

examples.ko: 제가 찾는 모델은 검은색이고 주머니가 많아요.
examples.romanization: jega channeun modeoreun geomeunsaegigo jumeoniga manayo.
examples.en: The model I am looking for is black and has many pockets.
examples.note: A complete shopping description.

examples.ko: 이 메뉴는 매운 음식을 좋아하는 손님들이 많이 찾는 메뉴예요.
examples.romanization: i menyuneun maeun eumsigeul joahaneun sonnimdeuri mani channeun menyuyeyo.
examples.en: This is a menu item often chosen by customers who like spicy food.
examples.note: Nested modifier clauses remain in front of their nouns.

examples.ko: 한 시간 동안 찾던 지갑을 소파 밑에서 드디어 찾았어요.
examples.romanization: han sigan dongan chatdeon jigabeul sopa miteseo deudieo chajasseoyo.
examples.en: I finally found the wallet I had been looking for for an hour under the sofa.
examples.note: 찾던 gives past ongoing background; 찾았어요 completes it.

본.nuance: 본 is the completed noun-modifying form of 보다: 어제 본 영화, 전에 본 사람. It means the seeing or watching happened before the reference point. 보는 is the present/habitual form (‘the movie I am watching / usually watch’), while 볼 is the future or intended form (‘the movie I will watch’). Because 보다 is vowel-final, -(으)ㄴ becomes ㄴ and attaches as 본. Do not build the modifier from the polite past 봤어요; Korean returns to the verb stem and attaches the modifier ending.
본.explanation: 본 (bon) means "that someone saw / watched" before a noun. It comes from 보다 + ㄴ. Compare 보는 영화 (the movie being watched), 본 영화 (the movie watched), and 볼 영화 (the movie to watch).
본.shortExplanation: 본 is the completed modifier of 보다; 보는 is present/habitual and 볼 is future/intended.
commonMistakes: Saying 봤는 영화. Completed modifiers use the stem: 보다 → 본 영화.
Using 보는 for a clearly completed event: 어제 보는 영화. Say 어제 본 영화.
Writing 보은. A vowel-final stem takes ㄴ directly: 본.
Confusing the modifier 본 with the noun 본 meaning ‘main/original’ in words like 본점. Context and following noun decide.

conjugationTips.title: 보다: 보는 / 본 / 볼
conjugationTips.body: Use 보는 for present or habit, 본 for completed past, and 볼 for future/intention: 보는 드라마 / 본 드라마 / 볼 드라마.

usagePhrases.en: a person I have seen before
the drama I am watching these days
the movie I will watch on the weekend

examples.ko: 어제 본 가방이 마음에 들어서 다시 가게에 왔어요.
examples.romanization: eoje bon gabangi maeume deureoseo dasi gagee wasseoyo.
examples.en: I liked the bag I saw yesterday, so I came back to the store.
examples.note: The viewing was completed yesterday.

examples.ko: 이 배우는 전에 다른 드라마에서 본 적이 있어요.
examples.romanization: i baeuneun jeone dareun deuramaeseo bon jeogi isseoyo.
examples.en: I have seen this actor in another drama before.
examples.note: 본 적이 있다 expresses prior experience.

examples.ko: 지금 보는 영상보다 어제 본 영상이 더 이해하기 쉬웠어요.
examples.romanization: jigeum boneun yeongsangboda eoje bon yeongsangi deo ihaehagi swiwosseoyo.
examples.en: The video I watched yesterday was easier to understand than the one I am watching now.
examples.note: Directly contrasts 보는 and 본.

사는.nuance: In this card, 사는 is the present noun-modifying form of 살다, ‘to live’: 서울에 사는 사람, 친구가 사는 동네. 살다 is an ㄹ-stem verb, so ㄹ drops before -는: 살 + 는 → 사는. The same written form can also come from 사다, ‘to buy’: 제가 자주 사는 물건. Context and nearby particles decide whether 사는 means living or buying. For a completed living period, 살던 is often natural (‘the place I used to live’), while 산 can mean ‘bought’ from 사다 or ‘lived’ in some completed constructions.
사는.explanation: 사는 (saneun) here means "who/where someone lives." It comes from 살다 + 는, with ㄹ dropping. Be aware that 사다 + 는 also becomes 사는, meaning "that someone buys."
사는.shortExplanation: 사는 can come from 살다 (living) or 사다 (buying); context decides, and 살다 drops ㄹ before 는.
commonMistakes: Writing 살는 사람. ㄹ drops before -는: 사는 사람.
Assuming every 사는 means ‘lives.’ In 자주 사는 물건, it comes from 사다 and means ‘often buys.’
Using 에서 with residence: 서울에서 사는 사람. Standard location with 살다 is 서울에 사는 사람.
Using 사는 as a complete sentence. Say 서울에 살아요 when no noun follows.

conjugationTips.title: 살다 → 사는
conjugationTips.body: ㄹ-stem verbs drop ㄹ before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ: 살다 + 는 → 사는. Compare 살아요 (predicate), 사는 집 (current residence), 살던 집 (former/remembered residence).

usagePhrases.en: a person who lives in Seoul
the neighborhood where my friend lives
usagePhrases.note: The subject 친구가 is inside the clause.
Here 사는 comes from 사다, not 살다.

examples.ko: 제가 사는 동네는 지하철역이 가깝고 조용해요.
examples.romanization: jega saneun dongneneun jihacheolyeogi gakkapgo joyonghaeyo.
examples.en: The neighborhood where I live is quiet and close to a subway station.
examples.note: Current residence with 살다.

examples.ko: 부산에 사는 친구가 맛집을 추천해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: busane saneun chinguga matjibeul chucheonhae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: A friend who lives in Busan recommended a good restaurant.
examples.note: Location 에 + 사는 + person.

examples.ko: 제가 자주 사는 커피는 편의점에서 할인 중이에요.
examples.romanization: jega jaju saneun keopineun pyeonuijeomeseo harin jungieyo.
examples.en: The coffee I often buy is on sale at the convenience store.
examples.note: Same form 사는, but this time from 사다.

입는.nuance: 입는 is the present/habitual noun-modifying form of 입다: 자주 입는 옷, 면접 때 입는 옷, 겨울에 입는 코트. It usually describes what someone wears regularly, in a certain situation, or as an ongoing action. 입은 is the completed/state-result modifier and often describes clothes someone has put on or is currently wearing: 검은 코트를 입은 사람. This distinction matters because clothing verbs can focus either on the habitual action (입는) or the resulting dressed state (입은). Pronunciation changes to [임는], but spelling remains 입는.
입는.explanation: 입는 (imneun) means "that someone wears / is wearing habitually." It comes from 입다 + 는. Compare 자주 입는 옷 (clothes one often wears) with 코트를 입은 사람 (a person wearing a coat).
입는.shortExplanation: 입는 is the present/habitual modifier of 입다; 입은 often focuses on the completed dressed state.
commonMistakes: Writing 임는 because that is how it sounds. The correct spelling is 입는.
Using 입은 for a routine: 매일 입은 옷. For habitual wear, say 매일 입는 옷.
Saying 입다 옷. Add the modifier ending: 입는 옷.
Confusing 입다 with 쓰다 or 신다. Clothes are 입다, hats/glasses are 쓰다, and shoes are 신다.

conjugationTips.title: 입다: 입는 / 입은 / 입을
conjugationTips.body: Use 입는 for present/habit, 입은 for completed/resulting state, and 입을 for future/intention: 입는 옷 / 입은 옷 / 입을 옷.

usagePhrases.en: the clothes I will wear tomorrow

examples.ko: 제가 회사에서 자주 입는 옷은 검은색 셔츠예요.
examples.romanization: jega hoesaeseo jaju imneun oseun geomeunsaek syeocheuyeyo.
examples.en: The clothes I often wear at work are black shirts.
examples.note: Habitual workplace clothing; 에서 marks the setting where it is worn.

examples.ko: 빨간 모자를 쓴 사람 옆에 회색 코트를 입은 사람이 있어요.
examples.romanization: ppalgan mojareul sseun saram yeope hoesaek koteureul ibeun sarami isseoyo.
examples.en: Next to the person wearing a red hat, there is a person wearing a gray coat.
examples.note: Contrasts clothing verbs 쓰다 and 입다 in result modifiers.

examples.ko: 여행 갈 때 입는 옷과 면접 때 입는 옷은 달라요.
examples.romanization: yeohaeng gal ttae imneun otgwa myeonjeop ttae imneun oseun dallayo.
examples.en: The clothes you wear when traveling are different from the clothes you wear to an interview.
examples.note: Same verb modifier applied to different situations.

읽는.nuance: 읽는 is the present/habitual noun-modifying form of 읽다: 요즘 읽는 책, 학생이 읽는 글. It can mean ‘is reading’ or ‘usually reads’ depending on context. The spelling preserves 읽-, but pronunciation changes to [잉는]. 읽은 marks completed reading (‘the book I read’), and 읽을 marks future or intended reading (‘the book I will read’). Do not form the modifier from 읽어요; attach the ending directly to the dictionary stem.
읽는.explanation: 읽는 (ingneun) means "that someone reads / is reading." It comes from 읽다 + 는. Compare 읽는 책, 읽은 책, and 읽을 책 for present, completed, and future reference.
읽는.shortExplanation: 읽는 is the present/habitual modifier of 읽다; spelling stays 읽는 although it is pronounced [잉는].
commonMistakes: Writing 잉는 because that matches pronunciation. Standard spelling is 읽는.
Using 읽은 for a book still in progress. 요즘 읽는 책 is the book you are currently reading.
Saying 읽다 책. The verb needs -는 before the noun: 읽는 책.
Assuming 읽는 always means ‘right now.’ It can also describe a habit: 매일 읽는 신문.

conjugationTips.title: 읽다: 읽는 / 읽은 / 읽을
conjugationTips.body: Use 읽는 for present or habit, 읽은 for completed reading, and 읽을 for future/intention. Pronunciations change, but spelling retains 읽-.

usagePhrases.en: the book I am reading these days
the news one reads every day
the book I will read next

examples.ko: 이건 제가 요즘 출근길에 읽는 소설이에요.
examples.romanization: igeon jega yojeum chulgeungire ingneun soseorieyo.
examples.en: This is the novel I have been reading on my commute lately.
examples.note: Current repeated activity.

examples.ko: 어제 읽은 기사와 오늘 읽는 기사의 내용이 달라요.
examples.romanization: eoje ilgeun gisawa oneul ingneun gisaui naeyongi dallayo.
examples.en: The article I read yesterday and the one I am reading today have different content.
examples.note: Contrasts completed and current modifiers.

examples.ko: 한국어를 배우는 사람이 읽기 좋은 짧은 글을 찾고 있어요.
examples.romanization: hangugeoreul baeuneun sarami ilgi joeun jjalbeun geureul chatgo isseoyo.
examples.en: I am looking for a short text that is good for Korean learners to read.
examples.note: Combines several modifier structures naturally.

먹는.nuance: 먹는 is the present/habitual noun-modifying form of 먹다: 자주 먹는 음식, 아이가 먹는 간식. It may describe what someone is eating now, usually eats, or eats in a certain context. The pronunciation is [멍는], but the spelling stays 먹는. 먹은 marks a completed eating event (‘the food I ate’), and 먹을 marks future/intended food (‘what I will eat’). In phrases like 먹는 약, it can also describe medicine taken orally rather than food.
먹는.explanation: 먹는 (meongneun) means "that someone eats / is eating." It comes from 먹다 + 는. Compare 먹는 음식, 먹은 음식, and 먹을 음식.
먹는.shortExplanation: 먹는 is the present/habitual modifier of 먹다; spelling remains 먹는 despite pronunciation [멍는].
commonMistakes: Writing 멍는 because of the pronunciation. The correct spelling is 먹는.
Using 먹은 for a regular habit: 자주 먹은 음식. Say 자주 먹는 음식.
Saying 먹다 음식. Add -는 before the noun: 먹는 음식.
Assuming 먹는 only refers to food. 먹는 약 means medicine taken by mouth.

conjugationTips.title: 먹다: 먹는 / 먹은 / 먹을
conjugationTips.body: Use 먹는 for present/habit, 먹은 for completed eating, and 먹을 for future/intention. Sound assimilation does not change spelling.

usagePhrases.en: the menu item being eaten now

examples.ko: 제가 한국에서 가장 자주 먹는 음식은 김치찌개예요.
examples.romanization: jega hangugeseo gajang jaju meongneun eumsigeun gimchijjigaeyeyo.
examples.en: The food I eat most often in Korea is kimchi stew.
examples.note: Habitual frequency inside a modifier clause.

examples.ko: 어제 먹은 음식이 너무 매워서 오늘은 안 매운 걸 먹고 싶어요.
examples.romanization: eoje meogeun eumsigi neomu maewoseo oneureun an maeun geol meokgo sipeoyo.
examples.en: The food I ate yesterday was too spicy, so today I want something mild.
examples.note: Completed 먹은 contrasts with present desire.

examples.ko: 이 약은 밥을 먹고 나서 먹는 약이에요.
examples.romanization: i yageun babeul meokgo naseo meongneun yagieyo.
examples.en: This is medicine that you take after eating.
examples.note: 먹다 naturally applies to oral medicine.

조용한.nuance: 조용한 is the noun-modifying form of 조용하다: 조용한 카페, 조용한 동네, 조용한 사람. With a place, it means little noise; with a person, it often means calm, reserved, or not very talkative rather than literally silent. The adverb is 조용히 (‘quietly’), so 조용히 말하다 describes how someone speaks, while 조용한 목소리 describes the voice itself. Since 하다-descriptive verbs take -ㄴ, 조용하다 becomes 조용한.
조용한.explanation: 조용한 (joyonghan) means "quiet" before a noun. Use 조용한 + noun, 조용해요 as a predicate, and 조용히 before an action verb.
조용한.shortExplanation: 조용한 modifies a quiet noun; 조용히 is the adverb ‘quietly.’
commonMistakes: Saying 조용하는 카페. Descriptive 하다 verbs use -한: 조용한 카페.
Using 조용한 before a verb: 조용한 말해요. Use the adverb 조용히 말해요.
Using 조용한 as a full sentence. Say 여기가 조용해요.
Assuming 조용한 사람 means someone who never makes sound. It usually describes a calm or reserved personality.

conjugationTips.title: 조용하다 → 조용한 / 조용히
conjugationTips.body: Before a noun: 조용한. As a predicate: 조용해요. As an adverb modifying an action: 조용히.

examples.ko: 온라인 회의를 해야 해서 조용한 자리가 필요해요.
examples.romanization: onrain hoeuireul haeya haeseo joyonghan jariga piryohaeyo.
examples.en: I need a quiet place because I have to attend an online meeting.
examples.note: A practical reason for seeking quiet.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 처음에는 조용한 사람처럼 보이지만 친해지면 말이 많아요.
examples.romanization: geu chinguneun cheoeumeneun joyonghan saramcheoreom boijiman chinhaejimyeon mari manayo.
examples.en: That friend seems quiet at first, but talks a lot once you get close.
examples.note: Personality nuance of 조용한.

examples.ko: 도서관에서는 휴대폰을 끄거나 조용히 통화해야 해요.
examples.romanization: doseogwaneseoneun hyudaeponeul kkeugeona joyonghi tonghwahaeya haeyo.
examples.en: In a library, you need to turn off your phone or speak quietly on calls.
examples.note: Contrasts adjective concept with adverbial action.

바쁜.nuance: 바쁜 is the noun-modifying form of 바쁘다: 바쁜 사람, 바쁜 날, 바쁜 시간. It describes having many tasks, appointments, or demands. It does not mean a place is crowded; for a crowded store, train, or street, use 붐비는. A shop can be 바쁜 when staff have a lot of work, but 붐비는 when many customers are physically present. 바쁘다 loses ㅡ before ㄴ and becomes 바쁜; the predicate form is 바빠요.
바쁜.explanation: 바쁜 (bappeun) means "busy" before a noun. It comes from 바쁘다. Use 붐비는 for a physically crowded place and 바쁜 for a person, day, or workload.
바쁜.shortExplanation: 바쁜 modifies a busy person/time; 붐비는 describes a crowded place.
commonMistakes: Saying 바쁘는 사람. The ㅡ drops and ㄴ attaches: 바쁜 사람.
Confusing 바쁜 and 붐비는. 바쁜 사람 has much to do; 붐비는 카페 has many people.
Using 바쁜 as a complete sentence. Say 오늘 바빠요.
Writing 바쁘은. The correct form is 바쁜.

conjugationTips.title: 바쁘다 → 바쁜 / 바빠요
conjugationTips.body: Before ㄴ, ㅡ drops: 바쁘 + ㄴ → 바쁜. Before -아요, it becomes 바빠요.

usagePhrases.en: I am a bit busy today.

examples.ko: 바쁜 시간에 연락해서 미안해요.
examples.romanization: bappeun sigane yeollakhaeseo mianhaeyo.
examples.en: Sorry for contacting you when you are busy.
examples.note: A common polite message frame.

examples.ko: 점심시간에는 직원도 바쁘고 식당도 많이 붐벼요.
examples.romanization: jeomsimsiganeneun jigwondo bappeugo sikdangdo mani bumbyeoyo.
examples.en: At lunchtime, the staff are busy and the restaurant is crowded.
examples.note: Directly contrasts 바쁘다 and 붐비다.

examples.ko: 이번 주는 일정이 많아서 너무 바쁜데 다음 주에 만나는 게 어때요?
examples.romanization: ibeon juneun iljeongi manaseo neomu bappeunde daeum jue mannaneun ge eottaeyo?
examples.en: I have a lot scheduled this week and am very busy, so how about meeting next week?
examples.note: Uses 바쁘다 while negotiating a more workable meeting time.

친절한.nuance: 친절한 is the noun-modifying form of 친절하다 and describes kind, considerate, or helpful treatment: 친절한 직원, 친절한 설명, 친절한 안내. It is not the same as 친한, which means socially close: 친절한 친구 is a kind friend, while 친한 친구 is a close friend. The adverb 친절하게 describes how an action is done, and the predicate is 친절해요. In service contexts, 친절한 often focuses on clear, patient help rather than emotional warmth alone.
친절한.explanation: 친절한 (chinjeolhan) means "kind / helpful" before a noun. Do not confuse it with 친한, "close." Use 친절하게 before an action verb.
친절한.shortExplanation: 친절한 means kind/helpful; 친한 means close in relationship.
commonMistakes: Confusing 친절한 친구 with 친한 친구. The first is kind; the second is close to you.
Saying 친절하는 직원. Descriptive 하다 verbs become -한: 친절한 직원.
Using 친절한 before a verb: 친절한 설명해요. Say 친절하게 설명해요.
Using 친절한 as a complete sentence. Say 직원이 친절해요.

conjugationTips.title: 친절하다 → 친절한 / 친절하게
conjugationTips.body: Before a noun: 친절한. Predicate: 친절해요. Adverb modifying an action: 친절하게.

examples.ko: 직원이 친절한 말투로 환불 절차를 설명해 줬어요.
examples.romanization: jigwoni chinjeolhan malturo hwanbul jeolchareul seolmyeonghae jwosseoyo.
examples.en: The staff member explained the refund procedure in a kind tone.
examples.note: Kindness appears through manner and help.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 친한 친구는 아니지만 항상 친절하게 대해 줘요.
examples.romanization: geu sarameun chinhan chinguneun anijiman hangsang chinjeolhage daehae jwoyo.
examples.en: That person is not a close friend, but always treats me kindly.
examples.note: Separates 친한 from 친절한/친절하게.

examples.ko: 처음 온 사람도 이해할 수 있는 친절한 안내문이 필요해요.
examples.romanization: cheoeum on saramdo ihaehal su inneun chinjeolhan annaemuni piryohaeyo.
examples.en: We need a user-friendly notice that even first-time visitors can understand.
examples.note: 친절한 can describe accessible information, not only a person.

필요한.nuance: 필요한 is the noun-modifying form of 필요하다: 필요한 서류, 필요한 정보, 도움이 필요한 사람. In a full sentence, what is needed takes 이/가 — 여권이 필요해요 — but before a noun, 필요한 directly marks the necessary item. Do not say 필요하는; 필요하다 is a descriptive 하다 word and becomes 필요한. In formal writing you may see 필요로 하는 (‘requiring’), but everyday speech usually prefers 필요한.
필요한.explanation: 필요한 (piryohan) means "necessary / needed" before a noun. Use N이/가 필요해요 in a full sentence and 필요한 N before a noun.
필요한.shortExplanation: 필요한 is the modifier of 필요하다; the thing needed takes 이/가 in predicate sentences.
commonMistakes: Saying 필요하는 서류. The correct modifier is 필요한 서류.
Using 을/를 with 필요하다: 여권을 필요해요. Say 여권이 필요해요.
Using 필요한 as a full sentence. Say 이 서류가 필요해요.
Overusing formal 필요로 하는 in simple conversation. 필요한 사람/물건 is usually more natural.

conjugationTips.title: 필요하다 → 필요한
conjugationTips.body: Descriptive 하다 words take -한 before nouns: 필요한. Predicate form: 필요해요. Adverb: 필요하게 is possible but less common than a clearer verb phrase.

usagePhrases.note: 도움이 is the subject needed by the person.

examples.ko: 신청에 필요한 서류를 미리 준비해 주세요.
examples.romanization: sincheonge piryohan seoryureul miri junbihae juseyo.
examples.en: Please prepare the documents needed for the application in advance.
examples.note: A practical administrative instruction.

examples.ko: 필요한 물건만 사려고 했는데 할인 상품도 샀어요.
examples.romanization: piryohan mulgeonman saryeogo haenneunde harin sangpumdo sasseoyo.
examples.en: I planned to buy only what I needed, but I bought discounted items too.
examples.note: Shopping scenario with 만 and intention.

examples.ko: 지금 가장 필요한 건 정답보다 충분한 설명이에요.
examples.romanization: jigeum gajang piryohan geon jeongdapboda chungbunhan seolmyeongieyo.
examples.en: What is needed most right now is a sufficient explanation rather than just the answer.
examples.note: 필요한 것 becomes 필요한 건 as topic.

중요한.nuance: 중요한 is the noun-modifying form of 중요하다: 중요한 일, 중요한 약속, 중요한 정보. It marks something as having high significance, priority, or consequence. In a full sentence, the important thing takes 이/가 — 시간이 중요해요. The adverb 중요하게 means ‘importantly / with importance,’ but Korean often prefers clearer verbs such as 중요하게 생각하다 (‘consider important’) or 중요하게 다루다 (‘handle carefully’). ‘Most important’ is 가장 중요한.
중요한.explanation: 중요한 (jungyohan) means "important" before a noun. Use 중요한 N, N이 중요해요, and 가장 중요한 N for the highest priority.
중요한.shortExplanation: 중요한 is the modifier of 중요하다 and marks high significance or priority.
commonMistakes: Saying 중요하는 일. Descriptive 하다 words become -한: 중요한 일.
Using 을/를 in the predicate frame: 시간을 중요해요. Say 시간이 중요해요 or 시간을 중요하게 생각해요.
Using 중요한 as a complete sentence. Say 이 약속이 중요해요.
Translating ‘important to me’ without a frame. Use 저한테 중요해요 or 저에게 중요한 일이에요.

conjugationTips.title: 중요하다 → 중요한 / 중요하게
conjugationTips.body: Before a noun: 중요한. Predicate: 중요해요. Adverb: 중요하게, often in 중요하게 생각하다 or 중요하게 다루다.

usagePhrases.note: The person for whom it matters takes 한테/에게.

examples.ko: 중요한 서류는 잃어버리지 않게 따로 보관하세요.
examples.romanization: jungyohan seoryuneun ireobeoriji anke ttaro bogwanhaseyo.
examples.en: Keep important documents separately so you do not lose them.
examples.note: A practical document-management instruction.

examples.ko: 저한테는 돈보다 자유 시간이 더 중요한 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: jeohanteneun donboda jayu sigani deo jungyohan geot gatayo.
examples.en: For me, free time seems more important than money.
examples.note: Personal value comparison with 보다.

examples.ko: 회의에서 가장 중요한 결정은 다음 주로 미뤄졌어요.
examples.romanization: hoeuieseo gajang jungyohan gyeoljeongeun daeum juro mirwojyeosseoyo.
examples.en: The most important decision in the meeting was postponed until next week.
examples.note: Superlative modifier in a workplace context.

만큼.nuance: 만큼 expresses an equal degree, amount, or extent: 친구만큼 빨라요 (‘as fast as my friend’), 필요한 만큼 가져가세요 (‘take as much as needed’), 생각만큼 어렵지 않아요 (‘not as hard as expected’). After a noun it functions like a particle and is attached: 친구만큼, 이만큼. After a modifying verb/adjective clause it behaves as a dependent noun and is spaced: 노력한 만큼, 먹고 싶은 만큼. Unlike 보다, which marks the comparison standard for ‘more/less than,’ 만큼 says the degree is equal or reaches that extent.
만큼.explanation: 만큼 (mankeum) means "as much as / as ... as / to the extent that." Attach it to a noun (친구만큼) but space it after a modifier clause (노력한 만큼).
만큼.shortExplanation: 만큼 marks equal amount or degree; noun+만큼 is attached, while modifier + 만큼 is spaced.
commonMistakes: Using 만큼 when you mean ‘more than.’ 친구만큼 = as much/as...as; 친구보다 = more/less than a friend.
Spacing noun + 만큼 as 친구 만큼 in standard writing. As a particle after a noun, write 친구만큼.
Joining a modifier clause and 만큼: 노력한만큼. As a dependent noun, write 노력한 만큼.
Building an incomplete comparison: 저는 친구만큼. Add the compared quality or action: 친구만큼 빨라요.

usagePhrases.en: It is not as difficult as I thought.
I do it as well as my friend.
Results come in proportion to the effort made.

examples.ko: 이 가방은 사진에서 본 것만큼 크지 않아요.
examples.romanization: i gabangeun sajineseo bon geonmankeum keuji anayo.
examples.en: This bag is not as big as it looked in the photo.
examples.note: 본 것 sets the degree expected from the photo; 것만큼 is written together.

examples.ko: 먹고 싶은 만큼 가져가도 되지만 남기지는 마세요.
examples.romanization: meokgo sipeun mankeum gajyeogado doejiman namgijineun maseyo.
examples.en: You may take as much as you want to eat, but please do not leave any.
examples.note: Quantity is limited by the desired amount.

examples.ko: 저는 언니만큼 한국어를 잘하지는 못해요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun eonnimankeum hangugeoreul jalhajineun mothaeyo.
examples.en: I cannot speak Korean as well as my older sister.
examples.note: Equal-degree standard inside a negative comparison.

어때요.nuance: 어때요 is the polite conversational form of 어떻다 and asks for an evaluation, condition, reaction, or opinion: 이 색 어때요?, 새 직장은 어때요?, 요즘 몸은 어때요? It does not ask for a method; 어떻게 means ‘how / in what way.’ The past is 어땠어요 (‘How was it?’), and the more honorific form 어떠세요 is common when asking about a respected person’s health, preference, or situation. In suggestions, N 어때요? means ‘How about N?’ — 다음 주는 어때요?
어때요.explanation: 어때요 (eottaeyo) means "How is it? / What do you think? / How about it?" Use 어떻게 for method and 어땠어요 for a past experience.
어때요.shortExplanation: 어때요 asks for an opinion or condition; 어떻게 asks how something is done.
commonMistakes: Writing 어떻해요. The correct form is 어때요; 어떻게 is a different word meaning ‘how.’
Using 어때요 to ask for instructions: 이거 어때요 해요? Say 이거 어떻게 해요?
Using present 어때요 for a finished event. Ask 어땠어요? for ‘How was it?’
Assuming 어때요 is always about quality. In 다음 주 어때요?, it proposes a time: ‘How about next week?’

conjugationTips.title: 어떻다 → 어때요 / 어땠어요
conjugationTips.body: 어떻다 is ㅎ-irregular. Present polite: 어때요. Past: 어땠어요. Honorific question: 어떠세요.

usagePhrases.en: What do you think of this?

examples.ko: A: 이 색 어때요? / B: 예쁘지만 저한테는 조금 밝아요.
examples.romanization: A: i saek eottaeyo? / B: yeppeujiman jeohanteneun jogeum balgayo.
examples.en: A: What do you think of this color? / B: It is pretty, but a little bright for me.
examples.note: Opinion request followed by a qualified response.

examples.ko: 이번 주는 너무 바쁜데 다음 주 화요일은 어때요?
examples.romanization: ibeon juneun neomu bappeunde daeum ju hwayoireun eottaeyo?
examples.en: This week is too busy, so how about next Tuesday?
examples.note: Schedule negotiation use.

examples.ko: 새 직장은 어때요? 아직 적응하는 중이에요?
examples.romanization: sae jigjangeun eottaeyo? ajik jeogeunghaneun jungieyo?
examples.en: How is the new job? Are you still adjusting?
examples.note: Asks about an ongoing condition, not a method.

고장 나다.nuance: 고장 나다 means a machine, device, vehicle, appliance, or system stops working properly. The broken item is the subject with 이/가: 휴대폰이 고장 났어요. 고장 내다 is the active/causative counterpart, meaning someone broke it. 망가지다 is broader and can describe physical damage, ruined objects, plans, or conditions; 고장 나다 specifically focuses on malfunction. Standard spacing is 고장 나다 because 고장 is a noun and 나다 is the verb.
고장 나다.explanation: 고장 나다 (gojang nada) means "to break down / malfunction." Use N이/가 고장 나다. If someone causes the damage, use N을/를 고장 내다.
고장 나다.shortExplanation: 고장 나다 is an intransitive malfunction (N이 고장 나다); 고장 내다 means someone broke it.
commonMistakes: Saying 휴대폰을 고장 났어요. The malfunctioning item is the subject: 휴대폰이 고장 났어요.
Writing 고장나다 as one word in careful writing. Standard spacing is 고장 나다.
Using 고장하다. Korean uses the noun + 나다 expression 고장 나다.
Confusing 고장 나다 and 고장 내다. 나다 happens to the device; 내다 means someone caused it.

conjugationTips.title: 나다 → 나요 / 났어요
conjugationTips.body: 고장 나다 follows 나다: 고장 나요, 고장 났어요, 고장 날 것 같아요. The active counterpart follows 내다: 고장 냈어요.

usagePhrases.note: Causative 고장 내다 when the speaker caused it.
A common next action after a breakdown.

examples.ko: 세탁기가 고장 나서 근처 빨래방에 갔어요.
examples.romanization: setakgiga gojang naseo geuncheo ppallaebange gasseoyo.
examples.en: The washing machine broke, so I went to a nearby laundromat.
examples.note: A practical household consequence.

examples.ko: 버스가 고장 나는 바람에 약속에 삼십 분 늦었어요.
examples.romanization: beoseuga gojang naneun barame yaksoge samsip bun neujeosseoyo.
examples.en: The bus broke down, so I was thirty minutes late for my appointment.
examples.note: -는 바람에 marks an unwanted cause.

examples.ko: 화면만 깨진 줄 알았는데 전원도 안 켜져서 완전히 고장 난 것 같아요.
examples.romanization: hwamyeonman kkaejin jul aranneunde jeonwondo an kyeojyeoseo wanjeonhi gojang nan geot gatayo.
examples.en: I thought only the screen was cracked, but it will not turn on, so it seems completely broken.
examples.note: Distinguishes visible damage from functional malfunction.

사장님.nuance: 사장님 is 사장 (‘company president / business owner’) plus the respectful title 님. In everyday shops, cafés, restaurants, salons, and small businesses, customers often call the owner or person running the place 사장님 even without knowing their name. In a company, 사장님 usually refers to the president/owner, not every direct supervisor; a supervisor may be 팀장님, 부장님, or 상사. When 사장님 is the respected subject, honorific particles and verbs commonly appear: 사장님께서 오셨어요, 사장님이 계세요.
사장님.explanation: 사장님 (sajangnim) means "business owner / company president" as a respectful title. It is common direct address in small businesses, but it does not mean every workplace manager.
사장님.shortExplanation: 사장님 is the respectful title for a business owner or company president, often used directly in shops.
commonMistakes: Calling every manager 사장님. A team leader or department head usually has a specific title such as 팀장님 or 부장님.
Dropping 님 when directly addressing the owner: 사장, 이것 주세요. Use 사장님.
Using 있다 for the respected subject in careful speech. Say 사장님이 계세요, not 사장님이 있어요.
Assuming 사장님 always means your employer. Customers also use it as a polite shop-owner address.

usagePhrases.en: Excuse me, how much is this?

usagePhrases.note: 께 and 말씀드리다 both mark respect.
Corporate use, distinct from a direct supervisor.

examples.ko: 가게에 들어가서 사장님께 예약 이름을 말씀드렸어요.
examples.romanization: gagee deureogaseo sajangnimkke yeyak ireumeul malsseumdeuryeosseoyo.
examples.en: I went into the shop and told the owner the reservation name.
examples.note: Respectful recipient and speech verb.

examples.ko: 사장님은 지금 안 계시고 다섯 시쯤 돌아오실 거예요.
examples.romanization: sajangnimeun jigeum an gyesigo daseot sijjeum doraosil geoyeyo.
examples.en: The owner is not here now and will return around five.
examples.note: Honorific 계시다 and 오시다.

examples.ko: 우리 팀의 직접 상사는 팀장님이고 사장님은 회사 전체를 맡고 계세요.
examples.romanization: uri timui jikjeop sangsaneun timjangnimigo sajangnimeun hoesa jeonchereul matgo gyeseyo.
examples.en: Our direct supervisor is the team leader, while the company president is responsible for the whole company.
examples.note: Separates workplace hierarchy terms.

고객님.nuance: 고객님 is 고객 (‘customer/client’) plus 님 and belongs to respectful service language. Staff use it when directly addressing or referring to a customer in stores, banks, clinics, call centers, delivery services, and online support. 손님 is broader and warmer for a guest or customer in a shop/restaurant; 고객 is more institutional, and 고객님 adds direct respect. Outside a service relationship, repeatedly calling someone 고객님 can sound transactional. When the customer is the honored subject or recipient, service language often uses 고객님께서 and 고객님께.
고객님.explanation: 고객님 (gogaengnim) means "customer / client" as an honorific service title. Use it in customer-facing communication; 손님 is often more natural for a guest or restaurant/shop visitor.
고객님.shortExplanation: 고객님 is a respectful service-register address for a customer or client.
commonMistakes: Using 고객님 for friends or ordinary acquaintances. It belongs to a service/customer relationship and can sound impersonal elsewhere.
Treating 고객님 and 손님 as identical in tone. 고객님 is institutional service language; 손님 is broader and often warmer.
Adding another 님, such as 고객님님. 고객님 is already honorific.
Using only plain verbs while heavily honorifying the noun. Service language usually aligns the whole sentence: 고객님께 안내해 드리겠습니다.

usagePhrases.en: to provide guidance to the customer
usagePhrases.note: 께 and 드리다 create respectful service direction.

usagePhrases.en: the details requested by the customer

usagePhrases.note: Written promotional/official noun phrase without direct address.

examples.ko: 고객님, 주문하신 상품은 내일 발송될 예정입니다.
examples.romanization: gogaengnim, jumunhasin sangpumeun naeil balsongdoel yejeongimnida.
examples.en: Your order is scheduled to be shipped tomorrow.
examples.note: Formal customer-service notification.

examples.ko: 고객님께서 말씀하신 문제를 확인한 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.romanization: gogaengnimkkeseo malsseumhasin munjereul hwaginhan hu dasi yeollakdeurigetseumnida.
examples.en: After checking the issue you mentioned, we will contact you again.
examples.note: Consistent honorific service register.

examples.ko: 식당에서는 손님이라고 많이 하고, 콜센터에서는 고객님이라고 자주 불러요.
examples.romanization: sikdangeseoneun sonnimirago mani hago, kol senteoeseoneun gogaengnimirago jaju bulleoyo.
examples.en: Restaurants often say sonnim, while call centers frequently address people as gogaengnim.
examples.note: Shows the register/channel difference.
